characters: Adom: 9-year-old Ghanaian girl with braided puffs and colourful beads, wearing a cheerful yellow-and-green dress and carrying a small idea notebook.
Grandma Akua: Warm, wise Ashanti grandmother wearing a patterned kente-cloth wrap and headwrap with gentle spectacles.
Auntie Serwaa: Respected Kumasi market trader in a vibrant orange-and-green wax-print dress and apron, with a sales notebook and baskets of fresh oranges and vegetables.

narrationPlan.voice: Warm, lively Ghanaian-English storyteller voice (Kore) capturing the bustle of Kumasi market and Grandma Akua’s wisdom
narrationPlan.pace: Clear developing-reader pace (about 110 words per minute)
notes: Make the market arithmetic on Page 4 clear and easy to follow.
Bring out Auntie Serwaa’s calm fairness and Grandma Akua’s warmth.

music: Kumasi Morning Market Piano (cheerful, gentle rhythmic piano accompaniment ducked beneath narration)
culturalNotes: Kumasi is home to one of West Africa’s largest open-air markets, where women traders have historically played a central role in commerce and community leadership.
Adom ("grace"), Akua (Wednesday-born) and Serwaa are traditional Akan names.
reviewQuestions: Are the market arithmetic problems (4 × GH₵15 = GH₵60; GH₵100 - GH₵60 = GH₵40) and the distinction between sales revenue and profit clear and accurate?
Does the historical note avoid overgeneralizing while recognising the diverse economic, political and community leadership roles of women across Ghana?

pages.brief: 3D animated vibrant Kumasi market scene. 9-year-old Adom in a yellow-and-green dress holds Grandma Akua’s hand among stalls of red tomatoes, sweet oranges and colourful Ghanaian cloths, looking admiringly at Auntie Serwaa arranging woven baskets of fresh vegetables.
pages.narration: Start with cheerful market calls, then warm curiosity between Adom and Grandma Akua.

pages.brief: 3D animated Kumasi market stall scene. Auntie Serwaa in an orange-and-green wax-print dress listens calmly and fairly to two customers beside baskets of produce while a young helper assists an elderly trader in the background and Adom watches with Grandma Akua.
pages.narration: Warm, respectful tone highlighting Auntie Serwaa’s fairness and problem-solving.

pages.brief: 3D animated warm living-room scene in Kumasi at evening. Grandma Akua and Adom sit on a sofa looking at a photo album showing historical black-and-white photographs of Ghanaian market traders and community leaders under warm lamplight.
pages.narration: Reflective, storytelling warmth as Grandma Akua shares the history of Ghanaian women in trade and leadership.

pages.brief: 3D animated market stall close-up. Four woven baskets of bright oranges sit on the counter while Adom smiles proudly and Auntie Serwaa shows her a ruled ledger notebook recording sales and expenses.
pages.narration: Crisp, lively pacing for the mental maths calculation and clear emphasis on recording sales and expenses.

pages.brief: 3D animated morning market scene. Auntie Serwaa kneels beside wooden crates of tomatoes, helping another trader sort bright fresh red tomatoes away from bruised spoiled ones while shaking her head at dishonesty as Adom observes attentively.
pages.narration: Earnest, principled tone as Auntie Serwaa defends customer safety and honesty.

pages.brief: 3D animated bright classroom and market crossover scene. Adom and her classmates hold neatly ruled handmade record books and colourful number charts, presenting them to a smiling Auntie Serwaa and grateful market traders.
pages.narration: Enthusiastic, collaborative tone celebrating intergenerational learning.

pages.brief: 3D animated school exhibition hall. Adom stands tall and confident beside a colourful display board with photographs and interview cards of Ghanaian women entrepreneurs, answering a visitor’s question while her teacher smiles proudly.
pages.narration: Confident, inspiring delivery on Adom’s answer about skills, opportunity and support.

pages.brief: 3D animated warm sunlit Kumasi market scene. Auntie Serwaa hands a bright new notebook to a beaming Adom while Grandma Akua stands beside her smiling warmly. Adom opens the notebook with excited determination.
pages.narration: Warm, uplifting conclusion as Adom opens her new notebook of ideas.

teacherGuide.overview: Discuss the contribution of Ghanaian women to trade without suggesting that all markets or traders operate in the same way. Invite learners to interview a local entrepreneur with permission. Use real-life calculations and explain that historical examples need supporting sources.
learningGoals: Solve practical multi-step market calculations involving multiplication (4 × GH₵15 = GH₵60) and subtraction for change (GH₵100 - GH₵60 = GH₵40).
Explain why money entering a business (sales revenue) is not automatically profit because expenses must be deducted.
Describe how women traders and entrepreneurs have contributed to Ghana’s economy and community leadership across history.

beforeReading: Ask learners what they notice when they visit a local market with their family and how traders keep track of prices and change.
whileReading: Pause at Page 2 for the quick question on what made Auntie Serwaa a respected leader.
On Page 4, let learners calculate 4 × GH₵15 and GH₵100 - GH₵60 aloud with Adom.
afterReading: Complete the five end-of-story activities covering the orange basket cost, change calculation, sales vs profit, traders’ contributions to society, and fair conflict resolution.
discussion: Why did Auntie Serwaa refuse to mix spoiled tomatoes with fresh ones even though it might have reduced short-term loss?
How did Adom’s class help local traders while also learning from them?
reflection: How can you practise honesty and fairness when helping at home, at school or in a community project?

mathsExtension.task: Four baskets cost GH₵15 each (GH₵60 total) and a customer pays GH₵100 (GH₵40 change). If Auntie Serwaa paid GH₵44 to buy and transport those four baskets, what is her actual profit?
mathsExtension.answer: GH₵60 sales revenue - GH₵44 expenses = GH₵16 profit.

support: Use play money or counters in denominations of GH₵10, GH₵5 and GH₵20 to act out the Page 4 orange basket purchase.
stretch: Design a simple 3-column record book page showing Date, Item Sold / Expense, and Amount (GH₵).

culturalNotes: Ghanaian markets have long traditions of female entrepreneurship and leadership; roles vary across regions, commodities and historical periods.
localiseThis: Invite learners (with parent/teacher supervision and permission) to ask a local trader or shopkeeper how they record sales and expenses.

investigation.title: Classroom Market Record-Book Design
steps: Draw three clear columns labelled "Item", "Money In (Sales)" and "Money Out (Expenses)".
Record the story’s sale of 4 baskets of oranges at GH₵15 each (GH₵60).
Subtract an example supplier and transport expense of GH₵44 to find the remaining profit (GH₵16).
investigation.whatToNotice: Keeping clear written records prevents confusion and shows the true difference between total sales and net profit.
investigation.safetyNote: Any interviews with local traders must be conducted with adult supervision and informed permission.

reviewerNotes: Confirm final vowel and nasal quality.
